summary: Sets the rules for how IANA assigns DNS parameters, such as resource record types, classes, opcodes, error codes, header bits, and AFSDB subtypes. This is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 2929 and updates RFC 1183 and RFC 3597. It was replaced by RFC 6195.

plainLanguage.summary: A big library needs rules for handing out new shelf numbers. This memo says how new labels for the Internet's phone book get handed out. It was later replaced by RFC 6195.

questions: how are new dns record types registered
what is the dns rrtype allocation policy
who approves new dns record types
subtitle: The rulebook IANA follows when it hands out new DNS record types, classes, opcodes and error codes.

tldr.problem: DNS has several numbered spaces (record types, classes, opcodes, response codes, header bits), and IANA needs clear rules for who may be given a new value and how.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists each numeric range and the policy that governs it, such as IETF Standards Action, IETF Review or Expert Review, and sets out a template-based process for new record types.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2929 and updates RFC 1183 and RFC 3597, but it was itself obsoleted by RFC 6195.

today: RFC 5395 is obsoleted by RFC 6195, so the current DNS IANA rules are there. It obsoleted RFC 2929 and updated RFC 1183 and RFC 3597.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) stores resource records under domain names, and its data is split into CLASSes and zones that can be maintained independently. RFC 5395 gives the general rules IANA uses when it assigns DNS parameters across query and response headers and all resource records.

Rules that apply to only one record type or one opcode live in the RFC that defines it. The one exception is the AFSDB record, whose rules are included here. The document obsoletes RFC 2929.
sections.plainLanguage: Many different number lists exist in DNS, and someone has to decide who can add to each list. This memo is the set of rules for that.

sections.title: Header Bits, OpCodes and Response Codes
sections.content:
Every DNS query and response starts with a header holding an ID, a QR bit, a 4-bit OpCode, flag bits (AA, TC, RD, RA, Z, AD, CD), a 4-bit RCODE and four counts. Some implementations copy the query header into the response without clearing bits, so giving a query bit a new meaning in responses, or the reverse, is dangerous. Such meanings may only be assigned by an IETF Standards Action. The same applies to the Z bit.

OpCodes 0 (Query), 1 (IQuery, obsolete), 2 (Status), 4 (Notify) and 5 (Update) are assigned, while 3 and 6-15 are available. New OpCodes need an IETF Standards Action as modified by RFC 4020.

The 4-bit RCODE looks small, but RCODEs also appear in OPT, TSIG and TKEY records. The OPT record gives a 12-bit field and TSIG and TKEY use 16 bits, all sharing one code space. The single exception is code 16, which means BADVERS in OPT and BADSIG in TSIG. New RCODEs in the open ranges need IETF Review, and 65,535 is reserved for IETF Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The top of every DNS message is a little form with tick boxes and a number saying what kind of message it is. Adding a new box or number needs a lot of approval because old software might misread it.

sections.title: Resource Record Types and the AFSDB Subtype
sections.content:
Every resource record has a NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA. TYPE is a 2-octet number. RRTYPEs fall into data TYPEs (which store data), QTYPEs (only for queries) and Meta-TYPEs (transient data tied to one message, such as OPT, TSIG and TKEY). Mnemonics must match [A-Z][A-Z0-9-]* and must not clash with CLASS mnemonics.

RRTYPE 0 is never allocated for ordinary use. Values 1-127 are for data TYPEs and 128-255 for Q and Meta TYPEs, both under the DNS RRTYPE Allocation Policy. Values 256-61,439 are data RRTYPEs under the same policy. Values 61,440-65,279 are reserved for future use, 65,280-65,534 are Private Use, and 65,535 needs an IETF Standards Action.

The AFSDB record has the same RDATA structure as MX, but its leading 16-bit integer is a subtype. Subtypes 1 (Andrews File Service v3.0 Location Service) and 2 (DCE/NCA root cell directory node) are assigned, 3-65,279 go by IETF Review, and 0 and 65,535 need an IETF Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of DNS record gets a number, like a jersey number on a team. Some numbers are saved for special jobs, some are open for anyone's private use, and a few are locked away.

sections.title: How a New Record Type Gets Allocated
sections.content:
An RRTYPE under the DNS RRTYPE Allocation Policy is allocated by Expert Review. IESG-appointed experts form a small pool, and IANA picks one for each application. Two requirements must be met.

  • A complete template (Appendix A) has been posted for three weeks to the namedroppers mailing list before the decision.
  • The record is either a data TYPE that can be handled as an Unknown RR as described in RFC 3597, or a Meta-TYPE whose processing is optional, so it is safe to discard it.

No less than three weeks and no more than six weeks after the template is formally posted, the Expert must post an acceptance or rejection. If no message appears, the application is considered rejected but may be re-submitted. IANA keeps a public archive of approved templates.

The Expert should normally reject a request that is unclear, incomplete, affects DNS processing without meeting the rules above, makes wrong assumptions about DNS behaviour such as wildcards, CNAME or DNAME, or asks for an excessive number of values when Private Use would do. Requests that fail the requirements may still be allocated by IETF Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: To get a new record number you fill in a form, show it to everyone for a few weeks, and a referee says yes or no. If the referee stays silent, the answer is no, but you can try again.

sections.title: CLASSes and Labels
sections.content:
CLASSes are another dimension of the DNS database: the same name can mean completely different things in different CLASSes. The assigned ones are IN (1), Chaos (3) and Hesiod (4), plus QCLASS NONE (254) and QCLASS * (ANY, 255). The text notes that the Internet CLASS, IN, has dominated DNS use and is the only CLASS in global use. CLASS 0 and 65,535 need an IETF Standards Action.

Values 5-127 are for data CLASSes by IETF Review, 128-253 for QCLASSes and meta-CLASSes by IETF Review, and 256-32,767 by IETF Review. The ranges 32,768-57,343 (data CLASSes) and 57,344-65,279 (QCLASSes and meta-CLASSes) use Specification Required, and 65,280-65,534 are Private Use.

Names are sequences of labels. There are two label categories, data labels and compression labels (pointers that shorten the encoding of names). The last label of every name is the zero-length ROOT label.
sections.plainLanguage: CLASS is like choosing which phone book you look in. Almost everyone uses the Internet phone book, so the others are rarely needed.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 2929
sections.content:
The IANA section lists the changes from its predecessor. Most "IETF Consensus" and all "Specification Required" policies for RRTYPEs become the "DNS TYPE Allocation Policy", while the remaining "IETF Consensus" entries become "IETF Review". RRTYPE 0xFFFF now needs an IETF Standards Action.

The OpCode rule adds "as modified by RFC 4020", RCODE 0xFFFF needs an IETF Standards Action, and a new registry is created for AFSDB subtypes. Specification Required CLASSes are split into data CLASSes and query or meta CLASSes.

The security section says the document is about allocation, not security, and points to the DNS Security documents.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the list of rule changes compared with the older rulebook, such as who needs to approve certain numbers.
